details:
Lua em Palavras ("The Moon in Words")

What it does / How it works

Lua em Palavras is an educational website that catalogs and explains the artificial objects humanity has left on the Moon's surface. Rather than presenting a dry list, the site tells the story behind each artifact — from scientific instruments (seismometers, retroreflectors) to the descent stages of lunar modules that served as launch platforms, and even personal items left by astronauts. Visitors can explore what each object was, why it was left behind, and whether it is still functional today.

Benefits

  • Makes a niche topic (lunar heritage) accessible to a general Portuguese-speaking audience.
  • Combines storytelling with factual detail, keeping readers engaged.
  • Fills a gap: most existing resources about lunar artifacts are in English and aimed at specialists (e.g., NASA's own catalogue).
  • Fully responsive and accessible from any device with no installation required.

Intended impact

The project aims to raise awareness about the cultural and scientific heritage left on the Moon, which is increasingly relevant as new space agencies and private companies plan lunar landings. By framing each object as a "word" in a larger story, the site positions the Moon not just as a destination for exploration but as a shared human heritage site worth understanding and protecting.

Tools, languages, and software used

Layer

Technology

Platform

Lovable (AI-assisted app builder)

Front-end

React + TypeScript

Styling

Tailwind CSS

Back-end / Hosting

Supabase (PostgreSQL, edge functions) via Lovable Cloud

Deployment

One-click publish to *.lovable.app

Authoring

Natural-language prompts (no manual code written)

Creativity

The project's creativity lies in its narrative framing: instead of a database or table of objects, each artifact is presented as a "word" contributing to a larger sentence about humanity's presence on the Moon. The title itself — Lua em Palavras — signals that the goal is to make the Moon's human history legible and emotionally resonant, not just factual. Additionally, the entire site was built through conversational AI prompting rather than hand-written code, demonstrating that meaningful, content-rich educational sites can now be produced without traditional development skills.

Factors the team considered

  • Language & audience: Written entirely in Brazilian Portuguese to reach the local educational and curious-public audience.
  • Accuracy: Content grounded in NASA's official catalogue of lunar artifacts and peer-reviewed sources.
  • Accessibility: Simple navigation, no login required, works on mobile and desktop.
  • Scope: Focused on why objects were left (deliberate vs. incidental) rather than just what was left, giving the site a clear editorial angle.
  • Sustainability: Hosted on Lovable's free tier, so the site can remain online indefinitely at no cost.
dataRefs: Apollo Lunar Modules: The descent stages of the Lunar Modules (like Apollo 11's Eagle) were left behind as launch pads.
https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1969-059C
Lunar Roving Vehicles (LRVs): Three electric "moon buggies" driven by astronauts. Parked permanently on the Moon.
https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1971-063C
ALSEP Scientific Packages: Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Packages (seismometers, retroreflectors, etc.) left to do science after astronauts departed.
https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1969-099C
Surveyor Landers: Robotic probes sent in the 1960s to prove soft landings were possible
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/surveyor-3/
Sojourner Rover: The first rover on Mars (1997), delivered by the Pathfinder lander. Now permanently parked.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/mars-pathfinder/
Spirit & Opportunity: Twin rovers that operated for years. Both are now inactive monuments to Mars exploration.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/mars-exploration-rovers-spirit-and-opportunity/
Viking 1 & 2 Landers: The first U.S. landers to successfully operate on Mars (1976), remaining exactly where they touched down.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/viking-1/
Phoenix & InSight Landers: Phoenix dug for water ice; InSight listened for marsquakes. Both eventually lost power.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/insight/
Dawn Spacecraft: Mapped Vesta and Ceres. Ran out of fuel and remains in a perpetual, unpowered orbit around Ceres
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/dawn/
NEAR Shoemaker: First spacecraft to orbit and land on an asteroid. Left resting on the surface of 433 Eros
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/near-shoemaker/
Pioneer 10 & 11: Early deep-space probes that explored the outer planets. Now drifting silently out of the solar system
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/pioneer-10/
Ingenuity Helicopter: The first aircraft on another planet. Sustained rotor damage and became a stationary artifact
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/mars-2020-perseverance/ingenuity-mars-helicopter/
Kepler Space Telescope: Revolutionary exoplanet-hunting telescope that ran out of fuel and is drifting in an Earth-trailing orbit.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/kepler/
